title: A Text Comprehension Routine for ELLs
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: A bilingual literacy interventionist describes her four-part comprehension routine for emergent bilingual students who enter with little or no English. The routine -- Vocabulary Preview, Multisyllable Reading and Spelling, Read/Read Back/Read Again with Visualizing and Verbalizing, and Summarizing -- deliberately leverages students' full linguistic repertoire. By discussing texts in Spanish while working through English, students reduce working memory load, lower anxiety, and express understanding at full capability rather than being bottlenecked by minimal English proficiency. The article walks through the routine step by step with a student who had under six instructional hours of English phonics instruction, demonstrating how vocabulary preview (targeting cognates and non-cognates), sentence-by-sentence reading with illustration-based comprehension checks, and bilingual oral summarization allow access to rigorous English texts from the very beginning of intervention.
points: * Vocabulary Preview targets two cognates and two non-cognates per lesson, building both cross-language pattern recognition and necessary background knowledge for non-cognate vocabulary. * The Read/Read Back/Read Again step is adapted from Lindamood-Bell's Visualizing and Verbalizing program: students predict what illustrations will show before viewing them, using Spanish discussion to deepen comprehension without using pictures as a crutch. * Discussing text in Spanish allows emergent bilingual students to deploy their full cognitive and linguistic ability rather than being limited to their minimal English vocabulary. * The Summarizing phase -- translating oral Spanish responses into written English together -- checks comprehension, reinforces vocabulary, and teaches students to distinguish key from extraneous information. * Comprehension is comprehension regardless of language: the approach positions linguistic flexibility as a cognitive asset, not a deficit.
quotes: Comprehension is comprehension, regardless of language.

Discussing the text in Spanish while working reduces the strain on students' working memory, lowers anxiety, and allows them to explain themselves to the best of their abilities as opposed to limiting them to their very minimal abilities in English.

Using cognates is very important for language learners because once they can hear the similarities between words in both languages independently, they will be able to recognize cognates automatically.

I have students first predict and explain in Spanish what they expect to see in the illustration and then check the image to confirm their comprehension, as opposed to using the picture as a crutch to help them make guesses.
Providing students with rigorous texts right from the get-go allows them to assimilate all these aspects of language, while also improving their English pronunciation while reading aloud.
Summarizing also helps students of any language background to learn the difference between key and extraneous information, formulate strong, concise sentences, and apply proper grammar while writing.
